sections.content: You know hedging with *al parecer* and *se dice que* (B2 Unit 18) and *parece que* (B2 Unit 21), and stance adverbs such as *lamentablemente* (B2 Unit 1). A news report uses them to show how far the writer stands behind a claim. The strongest claim has no marker: *El fuego está controlado.* *Según* + a source attributes it: *Según los bomberos, el fuego está controlado.* *Parece que* + the indicative reports an impression, and *no parece que* takes the subjunctive. *Supuestamente* and *presuntamente* mark a claim that is attributed or assumed but not proved. Add *oficialmente*, *de momento* and *hasta el momento* to say what is and is not confirmed.

sections.title: From stated to doubtful
rows: The fire is under control. (stated as a fact)
Según los bomberos, el fuego está controlado.
According to the firefighters, the fire is under control. (attributed)
Parece que el fuego está controlado.
It seems that the fire is under control. (an impression)
Supuestamente, el fuego comenzó en el almacén.
Supposedly, the fire started in the warehouse. (attributed, not proved)

items.spanish: Según los bomberos, el fuego está controlado.
items.english: According to the firefighters, the fire is under control.
It does not seem that there are any injured.

items.spanish: Oficialmente, las causas aún no se conocen.
items.english: Officially, the causes are not yet known.

items.spanish: Hasta el momento, no hay ninguna confirmación.
items.english: So far there is no confirmation.

sections.content: One marker is usually enough; each extra hedge weakens the claim. The press does stack them (*según fuentes, habría dimitido*), but a reader trusts a named source more than a vague one. English "allegedly" is a single word, and learners overuse *supuestamente*: prefer *según* + the source whenever you know it.
